analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to set mental health spending limits no lower than medical limits.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, introduced by 15 senators with 16 cosponsors, was referred to committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped employer health plans from setting much lower annual or lifetime dollar caps on mental health care than on medical or surgical care. Plans with a low mental health cap would have had to raise it to match the medical cap, or fold mental health into the same cap; plans with no medical cap could not impose one on mental health. It excluded substance abuse coverage, Medicare and Medicaid, and employers with fewer than 26 workers, and it left copays, visit limits, and other cost-sharing rules untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families covered by employer health plans who need mental health treatment and would otherwise hit a low dollar cap and pay the rest out of pocket. The bill's protections were narrow — dollar limits only — but for someone facing a $10,000 mental health cap beside a $1 million medical cap, the difference could be financially decisive.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with mental illness on employer plans

how_it_helps.text: A plan that caps mental health payments annually or over a lifetime below its medical or surgical cap would have to raise the mental health cap to match, or combine them into one shared limit [S2] [S3].
A plan that applies no dollar limit to medical or surgical care could no longer impose one on mental health care alone [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and the insurers and HMOs that run their health plans, which would have faced higher benefit costs when low mental health caps had to be raised. Some of that cost would likely surface in premiums or reduced benefits elsewhere, which is why small employers (under 26 employees) were carved out of the requirement [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill addressed only annual and lifetime dollar limits. Plans could keep discriminating against mental health care through higher copays, limited visits, or stricter medical-necessity rules, which the text explicitly permits as cost containment [S3].
Substance abuse and chemical dependency benefits were carved out entirely, as were Medicare and Medicaid plans [S3].
Employers with fewer than 26 employees were exempt, leaving out a large share of the small-business workforce [S3].
Requiring mental health caps to match medical caps raises plan costs, an expense that lands on employers and, through premiums, on covered workers themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections were real but narrow: equal dollar limits, while plans stayed free to discriminate through copays, visit caps, and care-management rules. The small-employer exemption and the substance abuse carve-out further shrank who was covered. Still, dollar caps were the most blunt and devastating form of mental health discrimination, and ending them would have mattered greatly to the families who hit them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Pete Domenici introduced the bill on August 2, 1996, with 14 other senators from both parties joining as original introducers [S3] [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day [S5].
Sixteen senators cosponsored the bill, eight from each party [S4].
The action record shows no further activity after the referral; the bill never came out of committee and received no vote before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, insurers, and HMOs were spared the requirement to equalize mental health dollar caps, and workers with mental illness continued to face the low caps the bill would have ended.

for.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Mental Health Parity Act of 1996 and recruited a bipartisan group of 14 co-introducers.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Joined Domenici as an original co-introducer of the bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its August 2, 1996 referral; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: 104th Senate
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after its introduction; no floor action appears in the record.

against.name: Employer and health insurance industry groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against mental health parity mandates, arguing they would raise health benefit costs, a campaign widely covered in reporting on the 1996 parity fight.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly bipartisan from the start: Domenici and Wellstone led, 14 senators co-introduced, and the 16 cosponsors split exactly 8 Democrats and 8 Republicans [S4].

industries.note: Low mental health dollar caps are a cost-shifting tool: the plan's liability stops and the patient's begins. The bill would have forced plans to raise those caps to match medical limits [S3].
Employers would have absorbed higher benefit costs, offset by better access to mental health treatment for their workforce; those with fewer than 26 employees were exempted [S3].
Raising the dollar caps would have kept more patients in treatment rather than dropping care when coverage ran out.
